title: What is refresh-ahead caching (proactively recompute a value in the background shortly before its TTL expires so regularly-accessed keys never miss), and how does probabilistic early recompute spread that refresh load so keys don't all refresh at the same instant?
shortTitle: What is refresh-ahead caching, and how does probabilistic early recompute help?

s1_definition.profdef: Refresh-ahead caching is a proactive strategy where the cache recomputes or reloads a popular value in the background shortly before its time-to-live expires, so a regularly-accessed key is refreshed while it is still valid and readers never experience a miss. This differs from plain expiry, where the value simply expires and the next reader suffers a slow miss that must reload from the source. The risk with any time-to-live scheme is that many keys expire at the same instant and a flood of readers all trigger reloads simultaneously (a cache stampede or thundering herd), hammering the database. Probabilistic early recompute solves this by having each read, as the value approaches expiry, refresh it with a probability that rises the closer it gets to the deadline, so refreshes are spread out over a window rather than all firing at the exact expiry moment, and only a small random subset of readers triggers the recompute while everyone else keeps using the still-valid cached value.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine the lobby displays today's gold rate, computed from a slow external feed, and the display is good for five minutes. With plain expiry, at exactly the five-minute mark the display blanks and the next customer who asks forces the clerk to run the slow computation while that customer waits — and worse, if ten screens all expire at once, ten clerks all run the slow computation together and jam the feed. Refresh-ahead is the clerk who, noticing the rate is almost five minutes old, quietly recomputes it in the back office a few seconds early so the screen never goes blank. Probabilistic early recompute is the clever twist: instead of every screen refreshing at exactly the same second, each screen rolls a dice that becomes more likely to say "refresh now" the closer it gets to expiry, so the refreshes trickle in spread across the last minute and only one screen actually triggers the recompute while the others keep showing the perfectly good current rate.
s1_definition.oneliner: Refresh-ahead recomputes a hot value in the background just before its time-to-live expires so readers never hit a miss, and probabilistic early recompute makes each read refresh with a probability that grows as expiry nears, spreading the refreshes over time so keys do not all reload at the same instant and stampede the database.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Refresh-ahead caching is a proactive strategy where the cache recomputes or reloads a popular value in the background shortly before its time-to-live expires, so a regularly-accessed key is refreshed while it is still valid and readers never experience a miss. This differs from plain expiry, where the value simply expires and the next reader suffers a slow miss that must reload from the source. The risk with any time-to-live scheme is that many keys expire at the same instant and a flood of readers all trigger reloads simultaneously (a cache stampede or thundering herd), hammering the database. Probabilistic early recompute solves this by having each read, as the value approaches expiry, refresh it with a probability that rises the closer it gets to the deadline, so refreshes are spread out over a window rather than all firing at the exact expiry moment, and only a small random subset of readers triggers the recompute while everyone else keeps using the still-valid cached value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine the lobby displays today's gold rate, computed from a slow external feed, and the display is good for five minutes. With plain expiry, at exactly the five-minute mark the display blanks and the next customer who asks forces the clerk to run the slow computation while that customer waits — and worse, if ten screens all expire at once, ten clerks all run the slow computation together and jam the feed. Refresh-ahead is the clerk who, noticing the rate is almost five minutes old, quietly recomputes it in the back office a few seconds early so the screen never goes blank. Probabilistic early recompute is the clever twist: instead of every screen refreshing at exactly the same second, each screen rolls a dice that becomes more likely to say "refresh now" the closer it gets to expiry, so the refreshes trickle in spread across the last minute and only one screen actually triggers the recompute while the others keep showing the perfectly good current rate.

**One line to remember:** Refresh-ahead recomputes a hot value in the background just before its time-to-live expires so readers never hit a miss, and probabilistic early recompute makes each read refresh with a probability that grows as expiry nears, spreading the refreshes over time so keys do not all reload at the same instant and stampede the database.

sections.s2_technical:
Refresh-ahead exists because plain expiry has a latency cost on every expiry. When a value's time-to-live elapses, it is gone, so the next reader gets a miss and must wait for the full reload from the source — a database query or an expensive computation — which for a hot key means a user-visible latency spike every time-to-live period. Refresh-ahead removes that spike for regularly-accessed keys by reloading the value proactively in the background before it expires, so the cache always has a fresh value ready and reads are always fast hits. The value never actually reaches the expired state for a popular key, because the refresh happens first. This is ideal for data that is expensive to compute and read frequently, like a computed dashboard, an aggregated rate, or a pre-rendered response.

Caffeine implements this directly with its refreshAfterWrite setting, which is distinct from expireAfterWrite. With expireAfterWrite, the entry is removed after the duration and the next access blocks on a reload. With refreshAfterWrite, the entry is eligible for an asynchronous refresh after the duration, but critically the first read after that point returns the existing (slightly stale) value immediately and triggers the reload in the background, so no reader blocks. You typically set a refreshAfterWrite shorter than an expireAfterWrite, so the value refreshes proactively while still having a hard expiry as a backstop. For example a Caffeine cache built with refresh after one minute and expire after five minutes keeps a hot key continuously fresh via background refreshes while guaranteeing a truly abandoned key eventually expires.

The danger that refresh-ahead and all time-to-live caching must guard against is the cache stampede, also called the thundering herd. If many keys share the same expiry time — which happens naturally when a batch of keys is loaded together, or when traffic spikes and many keys are cached in the same second — then they all expire at the same instant, and at that instant every reader of every expired key simultaneously misses and triggers a reload. The database is suddenly hit by a synchronized flood of expensive queries, which can overwhelm it and cause a latency spike or outage precisely when the cache was supposed to protect it. The problem is the synchronization: the load is not large on average, but it is concentrated into one instant.

Probabilistic early recompute (often called the XFetch algorithm) spreads this load by making the refresh decision randomized and time-dependent rather than a hard deadline. On each read, you compute how close the value is to expiry, and you refresh early with a probability that increases as expiry approaches. Concretely, each cached entry stores when it was computed and how long that computation took (its delta), and on read you draw a random number and check whether the current time plus a factor involving the computation time, a tuning constant beta, and the logarithm of the random number has passed the expiry time. The effect is that well before expiry the probability of an early refresh is near zero, and as the deadline nears the probability climbs, so a few lucky reads trigger the refresh early and spread across the window, while the vast majority of reads continue to return the still-valid cached value. Because the refreshes are scattered over a window and only a random subset fires, the synchronized flood is eliminated.

There are simpler variants of the same idea that are common in practice. One is to add random jitter to each key's time-to-live when you set it, so a batch of keys loaded together get slightly different expiry times and do not all expire at once — this is the cheapest defense and handles the "loaded together" case. Another is to combine refresh-ahead with a lock or single-flight mechanism so that even if several readers decide to refresh the same key, only one actually performs the reload (acquires the lock or the single-flight slot) and the others either wait briefly or return the stale value, which guarantees at most one reload per key regardless of reader count. Probabilistic early recompute and single-flight are complementary: the former spreads refreshes across time and keys, the latter ensures only one refresh per key at a time.

A senior nuance is that refresh-ahead trades freshness for latency: a reader may get a value that is slightly stale (up to the refresh interval old) in exchange for never blocking, which is a good trade for data where small staleness is acceptable but a latency spike is not. You must choose which data tolerates that — a displayed aggregate is fine, an authoritative balance for a debit is not. Another nuance is that refresh-ahead only helps keys that are actually read regularly, because the refresh is triggered by a read; a key that is not read will still expire normally, which is correct because there is no point proactively refreshing something nobody wants. A final nuance is cost: proactively refreshing consumes database and compute resources for values that might not be read again, so you apply refresh-ahead selectively to genuinely hot, expensive keys rather than to everything, and you rely on the read-triggered nature of the mechanism to naturally limit it to keys with ongoing demand.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India displays a computed portfolio valuation that is expensive to calculate from market data, and the team must keep it fast and avoid stampedes.

Problem 1 — With plain expiry, every time the five-minute time-to-live elapsed, the next customer's request blocked while the valuation recomputed, causing a visible latency spike on a hot screen. The team added refresh-ahead so the valuation recomputes in the background just before expiry and readers never block. This is refresh-ahead.

Problem 2 — Thousands of accounts' valuations were cached in the same burst at market open, so they all expired at the same instant and a synchronized flood of recomputations hammered the market-data service. This is the cache stampede.

Problem 3 — The team added probabilistic early recompute so each read refreshes with a probability that rises as expiry nears, scattering the refreshes across a window and ensuring only a small random subset recomputes while everyone else uses the still-valid value. This is probabilistic early recompute.

We will model a cache entry that records its compute time and expiry, a refresh-ahead cache that returns the cached value instantly and recomputes in the background near expiry, a probabilistic early-recompute decision function, and a demo showing a hot key never missing and refreshes spreading out instead of all firing at once.

The code will have a `CacheEntry` with value, computed-at, delta, and expiry, a `RefreshAheadCache` with a background recompute and an XFetch-style `shouldRefreshEarly`, a `ValuationService` as the expensive source, and a demo exercising a hot key and a stampede-prone batch.

```bash
javac RefreshAheadDemo.java
java RefreshAheadDemo

# Refresh-ahead (Caffeine): refreshAfterWrite(60s) + expireAfterWrite(300s)
#   → hot keys refresh in the BACKGROUND; readers get the current value instantly (never block).
# Anti-stampede:
#   per-key TTL jitter (cheap)               → batch keys don't expire together
#   probabilistic early recompute (XFetch)   → refresh prob rises near expiry; scatters load
#   single-flight / lock                     → at most ONE reload per key regardless of readers
# Apply selectively to genuinely HOT, EXPENSIVE keys (refresh is read-triggered).
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a portfolio valuation that is expensive to compute, read repeatedly over time, plus a batch of five keys cached at the same instant.

Step 1 — The first read of Rajesh's valuation is a miss, so the cache computes it from the expensive source, records when it was computed and how long the computation took, sets an expiry with a little random jitter added, and returns the value.

Step 2 — A read ten seconds later, well before expiry, is a plain hit: the probabilistic check says it is far too early to refresh, so the cache returns the stored value instantly with no recomputation and no database load.

Step 3 — As reads arrive near expiry — at forty-five, fifty-two, and fifty-eight seconds — the probabilistic early-recompute function rolls its time-dependent dice. Early in this window the probability is low, but as the deadline nears it climbs, so one of these reads triggers a background recompute. Crucially, every one of these reads still returns the current valid value immediately; the refresh happens behind the scenes, so no reader ever blocks.

Step 4 — For the stampede comparison, five keys are all cached at the exact same instant, which under plain expiry would make them all expire together and trigger five simultaneous recomputations. Instead, at fifty-five seconds the probabilistic function is evaluated for each, and because each draws its own random value, only a small subset decides to refresh early while the rest keep serving their still-valid cached values.

Step 5 — The result is that the expensive recomputations are scattered across the window and limited to a few keys at a time rather than all firing at the same instant, so the market-data source is never hit by a synchronized flood, and the hot valuation screen never goes blank or slow.

```
2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] === Hot key: refresh-ahead keeps it fresh, reader never blocks ===

2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] read @t+10s (hit, no refresh): ...
2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] === Near expiry: XFetch may refresh early in background, read stays instant ===
2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] read @t+45s: value=... earlyRefresh=false
2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] read @t+52s: value=... earlyRefresh=false
2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] read @t+58s: value=... earlyRefresh=true
2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] === Stampede: XFetch scatters refreshes vs all-at-once expiry ===
2026-10-24 17:37:02 [INFO] At t+55s only 1 of 5 keys chose to refresh early (rest use valid cache)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Refresh-ahead caching is a proactive strategy where the cache recomputes a popular value in the background shortly before its time-to-live expires, so a regularly-accessed key is refreshed while it is still valid and readers never hit a slow miss. Plain expiry has a latency cost on every expiry, because when the time-to-live elapses the value is gone and the next reader must block on a full reload, which for a hot key means a user-visible spike every period. Refresh-ahead removes that spike because the value never actually reaches the expired state for a popular key — the background refresh happens first and the cache always has a fresh value ready.

Caffeine implements this directly with refreshAfterWrite, which is different from expireAfterWrite: with expire, the next access after the duration blocks on a reload, but with refresh, the first read after the duration returns the existing slightly-stale value immediately and triggers the reload in the background, so no reader blocks. I typically set a short refresh interval with a longer hard expiry as a backstop, so hot keys stay continuously fresh while a truly abandoned key eventually expires.

The danger that all time-to-live caching must guard against is the cache stampede, or thundering herd: if many keys share the same expiry — which happens when a batch is loaded together or traffic spikes in one second — they all expire at the same instant and every reader simultaneously misses and triggers a reload, hitting the database with a synchronized flood that can overwhelm it exactly when the cache was supposed to protect it. The problem is the synchronization, not the average load.

Probabilistic early recompute, the XFetch algorithm, solves this by making the refresh decision randomized and time-dependent instead of a hard deadline. Each entry records when it was computed and how long the computation took, and on each read I draw a random number and check whether the current time plus a factor involving that compute time, a tuning constant, and the logarithm of the random number has passed the expiry. The effect is that far from expiry the refresh probability is near zero, and as the deadline nears it climbs, so a few lucky reads trigger the refresh early and scattered across a window while everyone else keeps using the still-valid value. Because refreshes are spread over time and only a random subset fires, the synchronized flood is eliminated. I pair it with cheaper complements — per-key time-to-live jitter so a batch does not expire together, and a single-flight lock so at most one reader actually reloads a given key.

In my banking work I used this for an expensive computed portfolio valuation displayed on a hot screen. Plain expiry caused a latency spike every five minutes and, worse, at market open thousands of valuations cached in the same burst all expired together and stampeded the market-data service. Refresh-ahead with Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite kept the screen instant, and probabilistic early recompute plus time-to-live jitter scattered the refreshes so only a few keys recomputed at a time. The nuances I always add are that refresh-ahead trades a little freshness for no latency spike, which is fine for a displayed aggregate but never for an authoritative balance used to authorize a debit; that it only warms keys that are actually read because the refresh is read-triggered, which is correct because there is no point refreshing something nobody wants; and that I apply it selectively to genuinely hot, expensive keys to control the extra compute cost.
